statins-common-questions-answered.name: Statins: common questions answered
statins-common-questions-answered.headline: Statins: what they do and the common concerns, as the NHS describes them
statins-common-questions-answered.summary: The NHS says statins lower the cholesterol the body makes, to reduce the risk of heart attacks and strokes, and they are usually taken long term.
keyPoints: Statins work by lowering the amount of cholesterol the body makes, which helps stop cholesterol building up in blood vessels.
The NHS says statins may be offered to people at higher risk of cardiovascular disease and to people who already have it.
Statins are usually taken long term, and the NHS says stopping can let cholesterol rise again.
Muscle pain, tenderness, weakness or cramps with no clear cause is something the NHS says to get medical advice about.
Grapefruit juice affects some statins more than others, so the NHS says to ask a pharmacist or GP about the one prescribed.
The NHS says that stopping a statin can let cholesterol rise again, so it advises talking to a doctor first.

body.heading: What do statins do?
body.body:
Statins are medicines that lower cholesterol.

Cholesterol is a fatty substance made by the liver and carried in the blood.

According to the NHS, statins reduce how much cholesterol the body makes. This helps prevent a build-up of cholesterol in the blood vessels. High cholesterol can lead to cardiovascular disease, which includes heart attacks, strokes and peripheral arterial disease.

Atorvastatin and rosuvastatin are two of the statins the NHS describes, along with others such as simvastatin and pravastatin.

body.heading: Who are statins for?
body.body:
The NHS says statins may be offered to people at higher risk of cardiovascular disease when healthy lifestyle changes have not helped or are unlikely to help on their own. They may also be offered to people who already have cardiovascular disease, to lower the risk of a heart attack or stroke.

NICE has published a patient decision aid, "Are statins the best choice for me?", for people weighing up whether statins are right for them.

The NHS says most adults can take atorvastatin, and that it is sometimes prescribed for children aged 10 and over. Caution is needed for people with liver or kidney problems or a past allergic reaction to a statin. The NHS advises against atorvastatin in pregnancy.

body.heading: How long are statins taken for?
body.body:
The NHS says statins are usually taken long term.

For atorvastatin, the NHS says it can be taken for many years and works best when taken for a long time. It says cholesterol should fall within about four weeks if the medicine is taken as prescribed.

The NHS advises continuing atorvastatin even when a person feels well.

body.heading: What side effects can statins cause?
body.body:
For atorvastatin, the NHS lists headaches, dizziness, nausea, muscle aches and digestive upset such as diarrhoea or indigestion as common side effects.

For rosuvastatin, the NHS says side effects often ease as the body gets used to the medicine, and that serious ones are rare.

The NHS lists rare serious effects including liver inflammation, pancreatitis, muscle damage and allergic reactions. It says yellowing of the skin or eyes can be a sign of liver problems, and that prompt medical attention is needed. For rosuvastatin, severe breathing or swallowing problems, or sudden swelling of the lips, mouth, throat or tongue, are emergencies for which the NHS says to call 999.

For rosuvastatin, the NHS says to contact a doctor if side effects last more than a few days or get worse.

body.heading: What about muscle pain?
body.body:
The NHS lists muscle pain, tenderness, weakness or cramps with no clear cause as possible signs of muscle damage. For rosuvastatin it says to get medical advice promptly if these happen.

For atorvastatin, the NHS advises contacting a doctor or NHS 111 straight away for these symptoms. The NHS says that if side effects are the reason someone wants to stop, the doctor may be able to change the dose or switch medicine.

body.heading: Do grapefruit juice and other things affect statins?
body.body:
The NHS says grapefruit and grapefruit juice can affect some medicines by raising the level of the medicine in the blood, which makes side effects more likely.

The NHS treats statins differently: grapefruit juice is a particular concern with simvastatin, while atorvastatin is affected mainly by large amounts and some other statins are generally not a concern.

The NHS also says drinking a lot of alcohol regularly increases the chance of side effects and liver problems with atorvastatin.

It advises talking to a GP or pharmacist about grapefruit if it is a regular part of the diet and a medicine that is affected has been prescribed.

body.heading: What does the NHS say about stopping a statin?
body.body:
The NHS says stopping atorvastatin may cause cholesterol to rise, which increases the risk of heart attacks and strokes.

It says there are no withdrawal symptoms and no evidence that atorvastatin is addictive.

For rosuvastatin, the NHS advises talking to a doctor before stopping because of side effects, since the problem may be unrelated to the medicine. The NHS also advises not stopping a medicine without advice.

how-long-antidepressants-take-to-work.name: How long antidepressants take to work
how-long-antidepressants-take-to-work.headline: How long antidepressants take to work, and what the NHS says about side effects and stopping
how-long-antidepressants-take-to-work.summary: The NHS says antidepressants usually start to help after 1 to 2 weeks and can take up to 8 weeks to work fully.
keyPoints: The NHS says antidepressants usually take 1 to 2 weeks to start having an effect and can take up to 8 weeks to work fully.
For sertraline and citalopram the NHS says it usually takes 4 to 6 weeks to work fully, with some people feeling better after 1 to 2 weeks.
Early side effects such as feeling sick, headaches and trouble sleeping are common, and the NHS says they usually ease after a couple of weeks.
The NHS and NICE both say that stopping suddenly can cause withdrawal symptoms, so changes to the dose are decided with the prescriber.
If a person or someone else is in immediate danger, call 999; NHS 111 (mental health option) and Samaritans on 116 123 (free, any time) are other routes.

body.heading: How long do antidepressants take to work?
body.body:
The NHS says antidepressants usually take 1 to 2 weeks to start having an effect. They can take up to 8 weeks to work fully. For sertraline, the NHS says it usually takes 4 to 6 weeks to work fully, although some people start to feel better after 1 to 2 weeks. For citalopram, the NHS gives the same pattern, with a usual 4 to 6 weeks before the full benefit and some improvement possible after 1 to 2 weeks.

Both medicines belong to a group called selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors, or SSRIs. For citalopram, the NHS advises against stopping after only 1 or 2 weeks just because it seems not to be helping, since the full benefit takes longer to appear.

body.heading: What can happen in the first weeks?
body.body:
The NHS lists nausea, headaches and diarrhoea among the common side effects of sertraline. It also lists dizziness or drowsiness, dry mouth and sleep problems. For citalopram, common effects include tiredness, feeling nervous, dry mouth and sweating. The NHS says common side effects like these are usually mild and go away after a couple of weeks as the body gets used to the medicine.

The NHS lists sexual problems, such as a lower sex drive, among the common side effects of citalopram. Sertraline can make a person feel more or less hungry than usual, so weight may go down or up at the start, the NHS says. The NHS suggests avoiding alcohol with sertraline because it can stop the medicine working properly. It also says grapefruit juice can increase the amount of sertraline in the body and the risk of side effects.

If side effects last beyond 1 or 2 weeks, the NHS suggests asking a pharmacist or doctor about them.

body.heading: What if nothing seems to change?
body.body: The NHS says a GP may recommend trying a different antidepressant if the first one is not helping. People respond differently to different antidepressants, so a change of medicine can sometimes help. Anyone worried about their progress can raise it with a GP or pharmacist.

body.heading: Why is stopping suddenly a question for the prescriber?
body.body:
The NHS says antidepressants should not be stopped suddenly, because this may cause withdrawal symptoms. For citalopram, the NHS says the doctor will usually recommend reducing the dose gradually over several weeks, or longer after a long course. For sertraline, the NHS says stopping is usually done by reducing the dose gradually.

NICE says reducing the dose in stages, known as tapering, helps to lessen withdrawal effects, and that the taper is agreed with the person's healthcare professional. NICE guidance for adults with depression also says people who want to stop should talk to the person who prescribed the medicine. Tapering is typically needed, and most people manage to stop successfully. The NHS adds that stopping too early can make depression come back.

body.heading: How long does treatment usually last?
body.body: The NHS says a course of antidepressants usually lasts for at least 6 months after a person starts to feel better. For citalopram, the NHS says most doctors recommend taking antidepressants for 6 months to a year. For sertraline, the NHS says most doctors recommend treatment for 6 months to a year after a person no longer feels depressed. The decision to stop or continue depends on symptoms and how well the medicine is working, and is made with the prescriber.

body.heading: Where can someone get help in a crisis?
body.body: If a person or someone else is in immediate danger, the NHS says to call 999 or go to A&E. For urgent help that is not an emergency, NHS 111 has a mental health option. Samaritans can be called free on 116 123 at any time of the day or night. In England, adults aged 18 or over can refer themselves directly to NHS talking therapies without a GP referral. These services are for anxiety and depression and are not for urgent crisis help.

warfarin-apixaban-medicines-and-food.name: Warfarin and apixaban: medicines and food
warfarin-apixaban-medicines-and-food.headline: Taking warfarin or apixaban: why other medicines and food matter
warfarin-apixaban-medicines-and-food.summary: Bleeding is the main risk of both, so the NHS says other medicines, alcohol and, for warfarin, some foods and INR blood tests all matter.
keyPoints: Warfarin and apixaban are anticoagulants, medicines used to prevent and treat harmful blood clots.
The NHS says the amount of vitamin K-rich food should stay consistent on warfarin, and that cranberry products and grapefruit juice are avoided.
Warfarin needs regular INR blood tests, which measure how quickly the blood clots.
Both medicines can cause bleeding, and the NHS says to call NHS 111 for symptoms of bleeding or after a head injury.
Anyone taking either medicine should check with a pharmacist before using other medicines, herbal products or supplements.

body.heading: What are warfarin and apixaban for?
body.body: Warfarin and apixaban are anticoagulant medicines, which are used to prevent and treat harmful blood clots. An NHS trust explains that warfarin works by blocking vitamin K, which is involved in the clotting process. The same trust lists apixaban among the direct oral anticoagulants, or DOACs, a different group of anticoagulants that NICE has approved for preventing stroke in people with atrial fibrillation, an irregular heart rhythm. Both medicines make bleeding the main thing to watch for, which is why other medicines and some food and drink matter.

body.heading: Does food or drink matter with warfarin?
body.body: The NHS says some food and drink can change how warfarin works. NHS inform lists green leafy vegetables such as broccoli, spinach and lettuce, chickpeas, liver, egg yolks, mature and blue cheese, avocado and olive oil as rich in vitamin K, which can interfere with warfarin. The advice is to keep the amount eaten steady rather than cut these foods out. Cranberry juice and cranberry products, and grapefruit juice, should be avoided, because they can increase the effect of warfarin and the risk of bleeding. NHS inform also says that getting drunk or binge drinking is dangerous on warfarin, as it may increase the medicine's effect and the risk of bleeding.

body.heading: Does food or alcohol matter with apixaban?
body.body: The NHS page on apixaban says it can be taken with or without food. On alcohol, NHS hospital leaflets differ in emphasis. One says heavy or binge drinking raises the risk of bleeding. Another says apixaban does not interact with alcohol and advises drinking in moderation within UK guidelines. A pharmacist or the prescriber can say what applies to a particular person.

body.heading: Which other medicines can interact?
body.body: The NHS says to tell a doctor, anticoagulant clinic or pharmacist about any new medicine, including products bought over the counter. For warfarin, the NHS says St John's wort, a herbal remedy, and vitamin K supplements should not be taken. For apixaban, the NHS lists other anticoagulants, some antifungal medicines and antibiotics, some heart-rhythm and epilepsy medicines and transplant medicines among those that can interact. It says St John's wort should not be taken with apixaban, and that there is not enough information to show other herbal remedies and supplements are safe, so a pharmacist should be asked. On painkillers, NHS advice says aspirin and anti-inflammatory painkillers such as ibuprofen increase the chance of bleeding and are not taken unless a doctor has said it is fine. The NHS apixaban page says paracetamol is generally fine. NHS trust leaflets for warfarin say occasional paracetamol is acceptable but regular or prolonged use can raise the INR. A pharmacist can advise before over-the-counter remedies or herbal products are bought.

body.heading: Why does warfarin need INR blood tests?
body.body: The NHS says warfarin treatment needs regular blood tests to measure how quickly the blood clots, called the international normalised ratio, or INR. NHS trust leaflets say tests are frequent at first and are spaced out once the dose is stable. The clinic uses the result to adjust the warfarin dose, and the target depends on the condition being treated. New medicines, antibiotics, illness with vomiting or diarrhoea and changes in diet can all shift the INR, so the anticoagulant clinic is told about them.

body.heading: What are the signs of bleeding, and who should be contacted?
body.body: Bleeding is the main risk of both medicines. For warfarin, the NHS lists blood in the urine or stools, unexplained bruising, and coughing up or vomiting blood as signs of bleeding. A sudden bad headache with confusion, slurred speech or difficulty moving the arms or legs can mean bleeding in the brain. For apixaban, the NHS describes bleeding more easily than usual, such as nosebleeds, bleeding gums, heavier periods and bruising. The NHS also lists a serious allergic reaction, with swelling of the throat or tongue and difficulty breathing, as a rare side effect of both medicines. The NHS says to call NHS 111 for symptoms of bleeding, after a head injury, or for other serious side effects. NHS inform says to call 999 or go to A&E after a fall, a significant blow to the head, or if bleeding cannot be stopped. For questions that are not urgent, the GP or anticoagulant clinic can advise.

body.heading: What if a dose is missed?
body.body: NHS sources give different timing rules for a forgotten dose, and the rules vary between warfarin and apixaban and between local services, so no single rule is given here. For warfarin, NHS inform gives separate advice for evening doses, and some local anticoagulant clinics allow a different window. For apixaban, the NHS says a missed dose is taken as soon as it is remembered unless the next dose is nearly due. The sources agree that two doses should never be taken together to make up for a missed one. If unsure about a missed warfarin dose, the GP practice or anticoagulant clinic can advise, and NHS 111 can also help. For apixaban, the NHS says to tell the GP if more than the prescribed amount has been taken.

ibuprofen-and-paracetamol-together.name: Ibuprofen and paracetamol together: NHS view
ibuprofen-and-paracetamol-together.headline: Can you take ibuprofen and paracetamol together? What the NHS says
ibuprofen-and-paracetamol-together.summary: The NHS says adults can take paracetamol and ibuprofen together if needed, but children should not be given them at the same time.
keyPoints: The NHS says adults can take paracetamol and ibuprofen at the same time if needed, and NHS inform says the two can be taken together if required.
For children, the NHS says paracetamol and ibuprofen should not be given at the same time but one at a time.
The NHS lists groups who should avoid ibuprofen or check first, including people with repeated stomach ulcers or bleeding, asthma, or severe kidney failure.
Many cold and flu products contain paracetamol or ibuprofen, so using several products can make it easy to take more than the recommended amount.
The NHS says to call 999 for signs of a serious allergic reaction, and to get urgent advice from NHS 111 or a doctor for other serious effects such as stomach bleeding or kidney problems.

body.heading: What is each medicine used for?
body.body: Ibuprofen belongs to a group of painkillers called non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, or NSAIDs. The NHS describes ibuprofen as a painkiller that also treats inflammation. It describes paracetamol as a painkiller for pain and high temperature. For a dental abscess, NHS inform says ibuprofen is the preferred painkiller, and paracetamol can be taken instead if ibuprofen cannot be taken for medical reasons. The NHS also says that if you need pain relief while taking warfarin, paracetamol is the one to take instead of ibuprofen.

body.heading: Can adults take both at the same time?
body.body: For adults, the NHS says paracetamol can be taken at the same time as ibuprofen if needed. It also says paracetamol can be taken with other painkillers that do not contain paracetamol, such as ibuprofen, aspirin or codeine. NHS inform, the NHS information service for Scotland, also says the two can be taken together if required. For a dental abscess, it says that if one painkiller does not work, taking both paracetamol and ibuprofen may help. The advice is different for children. For them, the NHS says paracetamol can be given alongside ibuprofen but not at the same time, and the two should be given one at a time.

body.heading: Who is told to check with a pharmacist or doctor first?
body.body: The NHS lists several groups who should avoid ibuprofen or check with a professional before using it. These include people who have had an allergic reaction to aspirin or other NSAIDs, with signs such as wheezing, a runny nose or skin reactions. They also include people who have had a hole in the stomach, bleeding in the stomach or a stomach ulcer more than once, and people with severe heart, kidney or liver failure. Asthma, hay fever and allergies are also on the NHS list. The NHS also says to avoid ibuprofen in pregnancy unless a doctor or pharmacist advises it, and to check with a pharmacist or doctor when breastfeeding. People over 65 are more likely to get stomach ulcers with ibuprofen, according to the NHS. Other medicines can interact with ibuprofen. The NHS interactions page lists warfarin and other anticoagulants, medicines for high blood pressure, steroids such as prednisolone, certain antibiotics and some antidepressants. It advises against taking ginkgo biloba with ibuprofen because it can increase the chance of bleeding. For other herbal products, it says there is not enough information to say whether they can be taken with ibuprofen. NHS inform advises anyone already taking other medication to check with a pharmacist first.

body.heading: Why do other products containing the same ingredients matter?
body.body: Many cold and flu products contain paracetamol or ibuprofen. NHS inform says this makes it easy to take more than the recommended dose. The NHS says to avoid taking other medicines that contain paracetamol at the same time as paracetamol, such as cold and flu remedies, because too much can be dangerous. It adds that taking two different medicines that contain paracetamol carries a risk of overdose, and that too much paracetamol can sometimes damage the liver. For ibuprofen, the NHS says to check the label of cold and cough remedies for aspirin, ibuprofen or other NSAIDs. Taking ibuprofen with other NSAIDs such as aspirin or naproxen is not advised without speaking to a pharmacist or doctor, because side effects such as stomach ache become more likely.

body.heading: What side effects do the NHS pages describe?
body.body: The NHS lists common side effects of ibuprofen as indigestion, stomach aches, feeling sick, being sick and headaches. Serious ones include stomach ulcers or bleeding in the stomach, and allergic reactions. The NHS also lists kidney problems, such as swollen ankles or blood in the urine, as a reason to get urgent advice. For paracetamol, the NHS says there may be no obvious symptoms at first after taking too much, so feeling well does not rule out harm.

body.heading: When should someone get help, and from whom?
body.body: For signs of a serious allergic reaction to ibuprofen, such as swollen lips, mouth, throat or tongue, fast or difficult breathing or a tight throat, the NHS says to call 999. The NHS also says to call 999 for severe chest or stomach pain, which can signal a hole in the stomach or gut, and for difficulty breathing or worsening asthma symptoms. Vomiting blood or black, tar-like poo can be signs of bleeding in the stomach, and the NHS says to get urgent advice from NHS 111 or a doctor. Swollen ankles or blood in the urine can point to a kidney problem, and the NHS says to contact NHS 111 or a doctor. If too much paracetamol has been taken, the NHS says to contact NHS 111 for advice, even when the person feels well. For questions that are not urgent, NHS inform says to speak to a pharmacist if unsure.

metformin-what-to-expect.name: Metformin: what to expect when starting
metformin-what-to-expect.headline: Metformin: what the NHS says to expect when starting it
metformin-what-to-expect.summary: The NHS describes metformin as usually the first medicine for type 2 diabetes. Side effects are mostly stomach-related and mostly ease.
keyPoints: The NHS says metformin is usually the first medicine prescribed for type 2 diabetes.
Common side effects are stomach-related; the NHS says most ease after a couple of weeks, and taking tablets with a meal or slow-release tablets can help.
The NHS says long-term use can cause vitamin B12 deficiency, so a doctor may check B12 levels.
The NHS says illness with vomiting, diarrhoea or fever risks dehydration, and metformin may need pausing before surgery or scans using dye.
For side effects, a GP or diabetes team can advise; the NHS says call NHS 111 for other serious side effects and 999 for suspected lactic acidosis or anaphylaxis.

body.heading: What is metformin used for?
body.body: The NHS describes metformin as a medicine used to treat type 2 diabetes, and says it is usually the first choice prescribed for it. It can also be prescribed to help improve ovulation in polycystic ovary syndrome, which the NHS pages call PMOS. The NHS says it reduces the amount of sugar the liver releases into the blood and helps the body respond better to insulin. The NHS also says it does not usually cause weight gain.

body.heading: How is metformin taken?
body.body: The NHS says metformin comes as two kinds of tablet: standard tablets and slow-release tablets. Standard tablets act quickly and may be taken several times a day, while slow-release ones work gradually, so they are taken less often. The NHS says the prescriber sets the amount, and that when standard tablets are first started the amount is usually increased slowly, which reduces the chance of side effects. It says it is best to take metformin with, or just after, a meal, and that tablets are swallowed whole with water rather than chewed. For diabetes, the NHS says treatment is usually for life, and that stopping suddenly makes blood sugar levels go up. The prescriber's instructions and the leaflet in the pack remain the guide for any one person.

body.heading: What side effects are common, and do they settle?
body.body: The NHS lists feeling sick, being sick, diarrhoea, tummy pain, loss of appetite and a change in taste among the common side effects. It says most of these should ease after a couple of weeks as the body gets used to the medicine, although some can last longer. The NHS says taking the tablets with a meal and increasing the amount slowly can reduce them. If side effects are too troublesome, it says a doctor may suggest slow-release tablets. Diabetes UK also says early stomach-related effects usually settle within a few weeks. For people on standard-release tablets who have these effects, Diabetes UK advises speaking to a GP or diabetes team, who can say whether slow-release tablets might suit them.

body.heading: What about vitamin B12?
body.body: The NHS says that taking metformin for a long time can lead to vitamin B12 deficiency, which can leave a person feeling very tired. Diabetes UK likewise says prolonged use, especially at higher doses, can lower vitamin B12 levels, which matter for red blood cells and nerves. The NHS says a doctor can check B12 levels in the blood, and that vitamin B12 supplements help if levels get too low. Diabetes UK says anyone with symptoms of deficiency should ask their diabetes team or GP about a blood test.

body.heading: What does the NHS say about illness, dehydration, alcohol and scans?
body.body: The NHS says that being ill with vomiting, diarrhoea or a high temperature while taking metformin carries a risk of dehydration. On alcohol, the NHS advises limiting how much is drunk while taking metformin, because alcohol can increase the risk of serious side effects, and says drinking more than its suggested limit can raise the risk of low blood sugar. The NHS also says a doctor may tell a person to stop metformin a few days before an operation or medical tests, and that it may need pausing before scans that use iodine-based dye. Anyone unsure what to do when unwell or before a procedure can ask a GP or pharmacist.

body.heading: Who may not be able to take metformin?
body.body: The NHS says most adults and children aged 10 and over can take metformin, but it is not suitable for everyone. Situations to raise with a doctor before starting include a past allergic reaction to metformin or another medicine, uncontrolled diabetes, liver or kidney problems, a severe infection, heart failure treatment or a recent heart attack, and heavy alcohol use. The NHS says metformin can be taken in pregnancy, alone or with insulin, after checking with a doctor, and that it can usually be taken while breastfeeding because only tiny amounts pass into breast milk. It also says there is no evidence that metformin lowers fertility in men or women.

body.heading: What if a dose is missed, or serious symptoms appear?
body.body: The NHS says not to take two doses to make up for a forgotten one. For side effects that are troublesome, the NHS says a doctor may suggest slow-release tablets, and Diabetes UK points people to a GP or diabetes team. The NHS describes serious side effects as uncommon and lists lactic acidosis (too much acid in the blood), anaphylaxis (a severe allergic reaction) and liver inflammation (hepatitis). It says to call 999 if lactic acidosis or anaphylaxis is suspected, and to call NHS 111 for any other serious side effect. NHS 111 is also the NHS route if more than the prescribed amount has been taken.
